take: Top five: Shiv Nadar & family, Gautam Adani & family (₹877 cr, up 127%), the Bajaj family, Mukesh Ambani & family and Nandan Nilekani.
125 self-made philanthropists (57% of the list) gave 65% of the money; 45 new entrants added ₹696 crore.
Rohini Nilekani (₹215 cr) is again the most generous woman; 29 women made the list, up from 24.
Only 47% of the total is personal wealth; the rest is company giving, including CSR, attributed by shareholding.
Delhi-based donors gave the most by value (₹3,168 cr); Mumbai has the most donors (64).
reports.act: Big family givers are growing fastest in health and climate — approach them as co-funders for CSR programmes there, and track your own unspent CSR closely.

reports.name: Catalytic CSR (Sattva 8th annual CSR report)
reports.sub: Where focused capital can move India's development needle
reports.org: Sattva Consulting and India Data Insights
reports.sample: Identifiable CSR projects of ₹25 lakh and above reported to MCA, FY 2022-23 to FY 2024-25
stats: CSR in FY25 — 15% a year compounded over the decade
Share of identifiable NCD-related CSR going to cancer vs cardiovascular disease, though heart disease causes over half of NCD deaths
Spent on exposure to the world of work for every ₹1 on academic and skills support (FY25)
To women's economic agency (29% of identifiable funding in the five areas); about 77% of it on skilling and livelihoods
Punjab, Rajasthan and Haryana's share of critical groundwater units vs their share of groundwater CSR
For innovation and research over three years; no industry gives it more than 1.2% of its CSR
take: NCDs now cause about 60% of deaths in India (up from 45% in 2004–06), yet CSR on NCDs is heavily tilted to cancer.
Youth unemployment rises sharply with education — 8.8% for higher-secondary vs 25.9% for graduates — so work exposure matters as much as more classes.
95% of groundwater CSR goes to recharge and source sustainability; demand management and water-use efficiency get little.
India spends about 0.84% of GDP on R&D vs 2.5–5% in leading innovation economies.
Three shifts: keep reassessing through data and learning loops, move closer to persistent needs other capital won't reach, and act as a multiplier through partnerships and technology.
reports.act: Use CSR's patience and appetite for risk on neglected gaps — heart disease, school-to-work exposure, groundwater demand and R&D.

reports.sample: MCA filings of 29,500+ companies; surveys of 67 CSR leaders and 200 non-profit leaders; interviews with CSR leaders from 31 organisations

Companies matching employee donations: India vs global

take: Place-based giving is concentrated: Tata Steel alone accounts for 41% of Jharkhand's CSR, and five mining and metals firms for 53% of Odisha's.
Accountability is seen differently: 82% of CSR teams say projects share accountability, but only 40% of non-profits agree.
Only 44% of the top 100 CSR spenders have a dedicated CSR head.
Social Stock Exchange interest is early: 67% of CSR teams open to it would route residual CSR funds through it.
India's corporate giving is 0.9% of corporate profits, within the 0.6–1.4% seen in the US, France and China; CSR is projected to cross ₹1.1 lakh crore by FY35.
reports.act: Fund multi-year, cover real overheads, and use employee giving to extend the CSR budget.

take: Private giving would have to grow above 25% a year just to stop the gap from widening.
Family giving is broadening beyond legacy causes to gender and inclusion, climate, livelihoods, arts and heritage, and animal welfare.
Women lead philanthropy in over 60% of giving families, and younger generations increasingly decide.
Investing in philanthropy infrastructure could unlock ₹1.25–1.35 lakh crore by FY30; institutions beyond the metros are the gap.
reports.act: Position CSR as catalytic capital: co-fund with families and government, and build NGO and intermediary capacity.
